Social crisis: Paris bans gatherings outside 10 high schools and 5 universities all week, education minister booed in Nantes

On the eve of the 17 November strike, the Paris police prefect has banned undeclared gatherings within 100 metres of ten high schools and five university sites until Friday. The UNEF student union is taking the matter to court. In Nantes, Édouard Geffray was booed at the Nelson-Mandela high school, set on fire on 1 October during a blockade [1][2][5].

The order, signed on 15 November by Patrice Faure, the Paris police prefect, bans undeclared gatherings and marches within a 100-metre radius of ten high schools and five university sites in Paris, from Monday 16 to Friday 20 November inclusive [1][3]. Schools in the inner suburbs are also affected [13].

The prefecture justifies the measure by saying that "a minority of pupils" are preventing everyone else from attending classes, and wants to avoid "numerous excesses and blockades"; the ministry is also asking prefects to station police outside high schools [3][4].

The UNEF student union accuses the authorities of wanting to "hand out fines left and right" and "crush the movement": in its view, the text defines neither what a gathering is nor from how many people. It sees a "manifest attack" on freedom of movement and freedom of assembly and has filed an urgent appeal with the administrative court [2][3].

On Monday morning, 20% of university institutions were disrupted, according to the office of Philippe Baptiste, the higher education minister [4]. On 3 November, the ministry counted 51 out of 184, a little under a third [8].

In Nantes, education minister Édouard Geffray was booed by pupils at the partial reopening of the Nelson-Mandela high school, and CRS riot police intervened [5][12]. "The Republic does not mean impunity," he said on site [14].

On 1 October, the fire gutted the entrance hall and damaged the canteen, seven classrooms and the boarding-house roof; the region released 850,000 euros to reopen part of the school, out of at least 4 million in repairs [6]. Two 16-year-old pupils have been charged and placed under judicial supervision; the prosecutor is appealing [7].
On Saturday 14 November, for the fifth Saturday in a row, 106,000 people demonstrated according to the interior ministry, 200,000 according to the youth inter-union group [10].

Key takeaway: the government is switching to a public-order response just as the movement is fading in the streets but not inside schools and universities. Banning every undeclared gathering around fifteen named sites for five days raises the question of the right to protest, which the administrative court, seized by UNEF, will have to settle [1][2][3].

The anger goes beyond schools: protesters denounce the cost of living, the state of public services, the lack of resources for education and a bill on the police, and the unions judged the boost to the minimum wage insufficient [9].

On Tuesday 17 November, young people join the civil service strike day: the civil service inter-union group, joined by the CFDT on 13 November, is demanding that the index point be unfrozen [9][11]. The week will show whether high schools and universities relaunch the movement or whether the firm line calms it down.

At the same time, Sébastien Lecornu's government has to get its budget through the Senate: every pay concession has a cost, and every day of blockades weighs on a university term already disrupted since early November [8][11].

If you are a high-school or university student in Paris, an undeclared gathering outside one of the targeted sites could get you fined until Friday. Declared demonstrations are still possible: for Tuesday 17, check the announced routes and disruptions to transport and schools.

Italy: Meta fined 805 million euros for digging into Android Facebook users' photos

Italy's privacy watchdog, the Garante, fined Meta 805 million euros, about 887 million dollars, on Saturday 14 November. The Facebook app on Android accessed photos, videos and their metadata without specific consent. Meta has 60 days to change its practice and says it will appeal [1][3][4].
According to the Garante, the Facebook app for Android accessed photos, videos and metadata stored on phones without specific consent or sufficient information [2][3].
At issue is the "Get suggestions from your gallery" feature, launched in 2023 and switched on by default: a single permission gave access to the whole gallery for several different uses [5].
The regulator estimates that about 20 million Android users were affected in Italy [3][4].
The fine represents about 0.47% of Meta's global revenue; the Garante held against the group its "lack of cooperation" and an earlier penalty, in 2019 [4][5].

The Garante found that Meta breached Article 122 of the Italian privacy code, which transposes the EU ePrivacy directive; Meta has 60 days to switch the feature off by default and ask for separate consent [3][4].
Meta says it "strongly disagrees" and will appeal: according to the group, users must first grant permission on their phone for the feature to work [3][4].
The investigation did not look at whether these images were used to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies [4]. The case was among Euronews's headlines on Monday [10].

Key takeaway: for Meta, 805 million euros is small relative to its revenue (0.47%), but it is one of the heaviest privacy fines ever imposed in Europe, just behind the 1.2 billion euros of 2023 [4][7].
The real stake lies elsewhere: the obligation to ask for separate consent, feature by feature, hits the heart of Meta's model, which lives off advertising and the data its apps collect [3][4].

The case touches a sensitive question in the age of AI: what the digital giants do with their users' personal content. The Garante did not investigate whether these images might have been used to train AI models, and Meta denies any such use [4].

If you have Facebook on an Android phone, you can check what the app can see: Settings, Apps, Facebook, Permissions, Photos and videos. The Italian decision applies only in Italy, but the same European rules apply in France.

How it works: why a record fine barely moves the share price

On the stock market, a fine is first read as a one-off expense, measured against the size of the company: 805 million euros is about 0.47% of Meta's annual revenue [4]. Investors mainly look at two other things. First the ceiling: under the European data regulation (GDPR), a penalty can reach 4% of global revenue [8], which sets the maximum risk. Second, and above all, what the decision forces the company to change: if Meta has to ask for separate consent for each use, some users will say no, and the company will collect less data to target its ads. It is this lasting effect on revenue, more than the cheque, that can weigh on the share. Finally, appeals take years: Amazon only lost its appeal against its 2021 fine in March 2025 [9].
Precedents: Europe's big fines against tech
June 2019
The same Italian Garante fines Facebook 1 million euros in the Cambridge Analytica case: an app had collected data on 214,077 Italians who had agreed to nothing [6].
That 2019 penalty weighed in the calculation of the 2026 fine, 805 times heavier [4][6].
July 2021
In Luxembourg, the CNPD fines Amazon 746 million euros over its targeted advertising, then a GDPR record [8].
Amazon appealed; Luxembourg's administrative court upheld the fine on 18 March 2025, nearly four years later, with a penalty of 746,000 euros per day for any delay [9].
May 2023
The Irish authority hits Meta with a record 1.2 billion euro fine for transferring Europeans' data to the United States, and orders it to stop those transfers [7].
Meta calls the decision "flawed" and says it was "singled out"; Amazon's 2021 record is broken [7].

news.2026-11-16-france-maileva-la-poste-: France: a cyberattack at Maileva, a La Poste subsidiary, exposes the names and addresses of 22 million people

La Poste announced on Saturday 14 November that Maileva, its mail-sending platform for businesses, was hacked in mid-September. The first names, surnames and addresses of 22 million recipients were stolen, and some letters may have been read. The CNIL has been notified and a judicial investigation is under way [1][2][4].

Maileva, a subsidiary of Docaposte, itself a subsidiary of La Poste, sends letters on behalf of companies and organisations: it is the contact details of the people receiving these letters that were stolen [1][4].
Its clients include social landlords, medical laboratories and hospitals; in Hauts-de-France, social-housing tenants may be affected [3][4].
According to franceinfo, "letters may have been read", though how many is not known [2].
Maileva has filed a complaint and notified the CNIL, France's personal data watchdog; all the affected client companies have been informed, according to the group [1][4].

Key takeaway: 22 million people are affected, and the leak hits a subsidiary of a state-owned group. Two months passed between the attack, in mid-September, and its announcement on 14 November [1][4].
The main risk is fake letters or messages using the name of a real organisation (landlord, hospital) to extract money or information [4].

In the coming weeks, be wary of any letter, text or e-mail asking you to pay or to give your bank details in the name of your landlord, a laboratory or a hospital: if in doubt, call the organisation on a number you already know.
